edition_title: BBC/Sky World Weather Bulletin - 26 November 2026, 20:30 UTC

stories.headline: Unprecedented 951 hPa bomb cyclone batters Iceland with 115 km/h gusts and landslide threat
stories.ticker: **BREAKING: Iceland bomb cyclone** - central pressure **951.5 hPa** - **#1 deepest in 87 years since 1940** /// Orange warnings across **north, east and southeast Iceland** - gusts near **35 m/s around Reykjavík**, up to **50 m/s east of Öræfi** /// Landslide and rockfall risk raised in Eastfjords after **10 of last 14 days** anomalously stormy /// Ring Road travel **not advised** in multiple regions tonight /// Climate shift: late-autumn severe gust frequency up from **3 events per decade** to **5 per decade** since the nineteen-eighties /// Unprecedented storm - **no comparable event since records began in 1940**
stories.voice_script: An extraordinary bomb cyclone, with a central pressure of nine hundred and fifty-one hectopascals, is tearing across Iceland this evening - the deepest late-November low pressure in eighty-seven years of records since nineteen forty. Gusts are approaching one hundred and fifteen kilometres an hour around the Reykjavík area, and near one hundred and eighty kilometres an hour east of Öræfi in the southeast. The Icelandic Met Office has issued orange warnings across north, east and southeast Iceland, advising people to stay indoors. Already-saturated ground is raising landslide and rockfall risk in the Eastfjords, and driving on the Ring Road is not advised in many areas tonight.
stories.region: Iceland, Reykjavík Capital Region, Southeast and Eastfjords

stats.metric_label: Gusts to 50 m/s east of Öræfi

cues.label: CYCLONE CENTRE
cues.spoken: At the heart of the system, central pressure has plummeted to nine hundred and fifty-one point five hectopascals - the lowest ever recorded here in late November.
cues.ticker: Central pressure **951.5 hPa** - **#1 deepest since 1940** for this date

cues.label: REYKJAVÍK AREA
cues.spoken: Around the capital region, gusts of thirty-five metres per second are bringing structural damage and forcing road closures across the Faxaflói Bay area.
cues.ticker: Reykjavík gusts **35 m/s** - Ring Road travel **not advised**

cues.label: ÖRÆFI SOUTHEAST
cues.spoken: Conditions are most extreme east of Öræfi in the southeast, where gusts of up to fifty metres per second have prompted orange warnings and advice to remain indoors.
cues.ticker: Southeast Iceland gusts **up to 50 m/s** - **orange warning** in force

cues.label: EASTFJORDS
cues.spoken: In the Eastfjords, heavy rain is falling on already-saturated soils, triggering a yellow landslide warning with rockfall and rapid river rises expected through Friday morning.
cues.ticker: Eastfjords **landslide warning** - saturated ground, **rockfall risk** rising

cues.label: ICELAND NATIONAL
cues.spoken: Temperatures are running nearly two degrees above the seasonal normal across Iceland - a signal consistent with the broader warming of North Atlantic storm tracks over recent decades.
cues.ticker: Iceland temperatures **+1.9°C above normal** - storm track warming confirmed

beats.title: Bomb Cyclone Batters Iceland Tonight
beats.text: A rapidly deepening bomb cyclone centred near Iceland at nine hundred and fifty-one point five hectopascals is driving the most violent late-November windstorm since ERA5 records began in nineteen forty. Orange warnings cover north, east and southeast Iceland, with gusts near one hundred and eighty kilometres an hour reported east of Öræfi. The Ring Road is closed in multiple sections, and the Icelandic Met Office is advising residents in the worst-affected areas to remain indoors.

beats.title: Ten of Fourteen Days Stormy
beats.text: This latest blast is not an isolated event. Ten of the last fourteen days have been anomalously stormy over the Iceland basin, with the two-week accumulated rainfall of eighty point four millimetres already nearly nine times the expected total. The repeated passage of deep lows has left ground across the southeast and Eastfjords fully saturated, amplifying the landslide and rockfall hazard with each new rainfall episode.

beats.title: Unprecedented: Number One in 87 Years
beats.text: The storm's central pressure ranks number one in the entire ERA5 archive for this date, covering eighty-seven years from nineteen forty to the present - an event at the ninety-ninth point four percentile. No late-November cyclone over Iceland has achieved a lower central pressure in the modern observational record, placing tonight's system in genuinely unprecedented meteorological territory.

beats.title: Warming Seas Fuelling Deeper Atlantic Lows
beats.text: Local autumn warming of nearly one degree Celsius since the nineteen-forties baseline, combined with record-warm North Atlantic sea surface temperatures through two thousand and twenty-six, is providing the energy source for more intensely developing cyclones in this region. The frequency of extreme autumn gust events over Iceland has risen from three per decade in the nineteen-forties to nineteen-seventies period to five per decade in the most recent forty years - a near-doubling that is consistent with what climate models have projected for a warming Arctic margin.

stories.headline: El Niño heats Peru's sea by 8°C as giant swells close 96 ports and threaten Lima coast
stories.ticker: **Peru coast emergency** - Navy closes **96 ports** from Tumbes to Tacna through **Sunday Nov 29** /// El Niño sea surface anomaly reaches **+8°C** off Lima - **2nd highest in 87 years since 1940** /// Wave heights **two to three times normal** peaking **Friday afternoon to Saturday** around Lima and Paracas /// Coastal sea level **51.1 cm above normal** at Callao - infrastructure damage in Miraflores, San Isidro, Chorrillos /// **28 of last 28 days** have recorded above-normal coastal heat - anomaly persisting all month /// Climate signal: coastal El Niño heat events now **six times per decade** vs just **once per decade** in the nineteen-forties
stories.voice_script: Peru's Pacific coast is bracing for its worst swell event in years tonight, as the Peruvian Navy warns that waves two to three times normal height will peak along the Lima coastline through Saturday. The crisis is being driven by an extraordinary El Niño sea surface temperature anomaly of up to eight degrees Celsius above normal - the second highest for this date in eighty-seven years of ERA5 records since nineteen forty. Ninety-six ports remain closed from Tumbes to Tacna. Coastal infrastructure in the Miraflores, San Isidro and Chorrillos districts of Lima has already sustained damage, and beach access is restricted under red-flag warnings tonight.
stories.region: Peruvian Pacific Coast, Lima, Callao and Paracas

cues.label: EL NIÑO HOTSPOT
cues.spoken: Far offshore, the El Niño hotspot has pushed sea surface temperatures to seven and a half degrees above the seasonal normal - a reading that ranks second in eighty-seven years of records for this calendar date.
cues.ticker: Pacific El Niño hotspot **+7.5°C** - **#2 in 87 years since 1940**

cues.label: NORTHERN COAST
cues.spoken: Along the northern coast from Tumbes to Salaverry, moderate swells are building today, with the navy warning small vessels to remain in port as conditions deteriorate ahead of the weekend peak.
cues.ticker: Northern Peru coast **ports closed** - swells building through **Friday**

cues.label: LIMA AND CALLAO
cues.spoken: At Lima and Callao, the sea level stands fifty-one centimetres above normal, and waves two to three times their usual height are battering coastal promenades, forcing the closure of the Costa Verde road.
cues.ticker: Lima sea level **+51.1 cm** at Callao - Costa Verde road **closed**

cues.label: PARACAS AND SOUTH
cues.spoken: South of Lima, Paracas and the Ballestas Islands boat tour sector are under the strongest swell warning through Saturday, with all maritime access suspended.
cues.ticker: Paracas **all maritime access suspended** - peak swells **Friday to Saturday**

cues.label: CENTRAL PERU COAST
cues.spoken: High pressure overhead is locking in hot, dry conditions on land whilst funnelling energy from the warm Pacific into the swell field - a classic El Niño Costero signature that Peruvian forecasters say has reached its highest intensity since this event began.
cues.ticker: El Niño Costero at **peak 2026 intensity** - warmest coastal seas since event began

beats.title: Ninety-Six Ports Closed as Giant Swells Strike Lima
beats.text: Peru's navy has extended a national swell emergency through Sunday the twenty-ninth of November, with ninety-six ports and coves closed from Tumbes in the far north to Tacna on the Chilean border. Wave heights of two to three times normal are expected to peak along the Lima and Paracas coast on Friday afternoon and Saturday. Coastal infrastructure in the Miraflores, San Isidro and Chorrillos districts of Lima has already been damaged, and traffic on the Costa Verde seafront road has been suspended.

beats.title: Twenty-Eight Consecutive Days of Coastal Heat
beats.text: Every single one of the last twenty-eight days has recorded above-normal sea surface temperatures off the Peruvian coast. The fourteen-day rainfall total stands at just four millimetres against an expected twelve-point-eight millimetres, confirming the characteristic El Niño pattern of coastal heat without meaningful relief from rainfall. Peru's official El Niño monitoring commission ENFEN confirmed on the thirteenth of November that coastal ocean warming had reached its highest surface intensity since the current event began in March of this year.

beats.title: Second Highest Sea Temperature Anomaly in 87 Years
beats.text: The coastal sea surface temperature anomaly of seven and a half degrees Celsius ranks second in the ERA5 archive for this calendar date, covering eighty-seven years from nineteen forty. At the ninety-eighth point three percentile, this places the current event among the most extreme late-November coastal El Niño episodes ever recorded. NOAA forecasters have warned the event could reach historic strength during the two thousand and twenty-six to twenty-seven season.

beats.title: El Niño Coastal Extremes Multiplying With Climate Change
beats.text: The local seasonal warming of zero point four degrees Celsius along the Peruvian coast since the nineteen-forties baseline appears modest, but the effect on extreme El Niño events is profound. The frequency of extreme coastal heat exceedances has increased from just once per decade in the nineteen-forties to nineteen-seventies period to six times per decade in the most recent forty years. Peru's emergency declaration covering nearly three-quarters of the country's districts reflects how vulnerable coastal communities now are to these compounding ocean-atmosphere extremes.

stories.headline: Bolivia declares El Niño emergency as 163 mm Amazon downpour floods communities and roads
stories.ticker: **Bolivia El Niño emergency** declared by President Paz - **78,000 families** hit by drought across **six departments** /// Amazon headwaters receive **163 mm in 24 hours** - **#7 in 87 years since 1940** for this date, 92nd percentile /// **127 mm** of rain has fallen in just **28 days** vs an expected total of under **12 mm** /// Flooded roads and rivers cutting off communities across **Beni, Pando and La Paz** departments /// El Niño combining **flood and drought simultaneously** across different Bolivian regions /// **GDACS Orange Alert** - drought affecting Aruba through Venezuela corridor since **September 2022**
stories.voice_script: Bolivia is in a state of national emergency tonight, with President Rodrigo Paz having declared the crisis at the end of October as El Niño drives a devastating combination of floods and drought across the country. In the western Amazon headwaters, one hundred and sixty-three millimetres of rain has fallen in just twenty-four hours - nearly fourteen times the daily average - ranking seventh in eighty-seven years of records. Drought is already affecting seventy-eight thousand families in six of Bolivia's nine departments. Emergency teams have been deployed to communities cut off by flooded Amazon rivers and collapsed roads.
stories.region: Bolivian Western Amazon, Beni and Pando Departments

stats.metric_label: 127 mm in last 28 days vs 12 mm expected
stats.persistence: 2 of last 14 days anomalously wet, intense bursts

cues.label: AMAZON HEADWATERS
cues.spoken: In the Amazon headwaters region of western Bolivia, one hundred and sixty-three millimetres of rain has fallen in twenty-four hours - nearly fourteen times the November daily average and the seventh highest reading for this date in eighty-seven years.
cues.ticker: Amazon headwaters **163 mm in 24 hours** - **#7 in 87 years since 1940**

cues.label: PANDO DEPARTMENT
cues.spoken: In the Pando department - Bolivia's northernmost Amazon territory - rivers are rising rapidly, with wet-season flooding beginning to restrict road and air access to remote communities.
cues.ticker: Pando department rivers **rising rapidly** - road access **restricted**

cues.label: BENI LOWLANDS
cues.spoken: In the Beni lowlands, below-normal temperatures and persistent heavy rain are flooding the Llanos de Moxos wetlands well ahead of their typical peak, compounding the emergency declared by the government.
cues.ticker: Beni lowlands **flooding early** - Llanos de Moxos wetlands **inundated**

cues.label: LA PAZ FOOTHILLS
cues.spoken: An elevated pressure pattern over the Andes foothills is channelling moisture-laden air from the Amazon basin into the highlands, triggering landslides and flash flooding on roads that connect La Paz with the tropical lowlands.
cues.ticker: La Paz to Amazon roads **hit by landslides** - Andes foothills on alert

cues.label: SANTA CRUZ REGION
cues.spoken: Further south in the Santa Cruz region, the twenty-eight-day rainfall total has reached one hundred and twenty-seven millimetres against an expected figure of under twelve millimetres - more than ten times the climatological average for this period.
cues.ticker: Santa Cruz region **127 mm in 28 days** - over **10× the seasonal average**

beats.title: National Emergency as Amazon Floods Cut Off Communities
beats.text: President Rodrigo Paz declared a national state of emergency on the thirty-first of October, with rescue teams deployed across Bolivia as El Niño simultaneously produces catastrophic flooding in the Amazon north and devastating drought across six Andean and southern departments. One hundred and sixty-three millimetres of rain has fallen in twenty-four hours in the western Amazon headwaters. Roads connecting the Amazon lowlands to La Paz have been closed by landslides, and river crossings in Beni and Pando departments are impassable in many areas tonight.

beats.title: Twenty-Eight-Day Deluge More Than Ten Times Normal
beats.text: Although the wettest days have been concentrated in intense bursts rather than a sustained wet spell, the cumulative impact has been severe. The twenty-eight-day rainfall total in the Amazon headwaters stands at one hundred and twenty-seven millimetres - more than ten times the expected figure of under twelve millimetres for this period. Bolivia's annual rainy season typically begins in November, but the scale and violence of this year's onset, amplified by El Niño, is exceptional by historical standards.

beats.title: Seventh Heaviest Daily Rain in 87 Years
beats.text: The twenty-four-hour rainfall total of one hundred and sixty-three point three millimetres ranks seventh in the ERA5 archive for this exact calendar date at the western Amazon headwaters location, placing it at the ninety-second point five percentile. The seasonal normal for a full day's rain in November here is just eleven point eight millimetres, meaning this single storm delivered more than thirteen times the climatological daily expectation.

beats.title: El Niño and Warming Accelerate Bolivia's Flood-Drought Paradox
beats.text: Local warming of one point seven degrees Celsius since the nineteen-forties baseline, combined with the ongoing El Niño event that NOAA has flagged as potentially heading toward historic strength, is intensifying the flood-drought paradox that Bolivia now faces each wet season. The government's emergency decree acknowledges the growing frequency and severity of this pattern, covering risks including droughts, floods, frosts, hailstorms, forest fires and river overflows through the two thousand and twenty-six to twenty-seven El Niño period.

stories.headline: Chad and Sahel bake in historic 30°C heat dome - seven degrees above normal for four weeks
stories.ticker: **Chad and central Africa heat emergency** - temperatures **30.4°C** - **+7.3°C above November normal** /// **Unprecedented: #1 in 87 years since 1940** for this date across the region, **99.4th percentile** /// **28 of 28 days** have been anomalously hot - **not a single cool day** in four weeks /// **Zero rainfall** in last 14 days against an expected **12.9 mm** - Sahel drought deepening /// GDACS **Orange Drought Alert** active - East and Central Africa impacted since **May 2026** /// Climate shift: regional heat extremes now **seven times per decade** vs just **twice per decade** in the nineteen-forties
stories.voice_script: An extraordinary heat dome is parked across Chad and central Africa tonight, pushing temperatures to thirty point four degrees Celsius - seven point three degrees above the late-November seasonal normal. This is the highest temperature anomaly ever recorded for this date across the region in eighty-seven years of records since nineteen forty. The heat has persisted without a single break for all twenty-eight days of the past month, with virtually no rainfall recorded. This unrelenting warmth is compounding the GDACS Orange drought alert that has covered the broader central African region since May, threatening food security and water access for millions of people across the Sahel.
stories.region: Chad, Lake Chad Basin, Central African Sahel

cues.label: CHAD HEAT DOME CORE
cues.spoken: At the core of the heat dome, centred over central Chad, temperatures are running seven point three degrees Celsius above the late-November seasonal normal - a reading that has never been exceeded in eighty-seven years of records for this date.
cues.ticker: Chad heat dome core **+7.3°C** - **unprecedented in 87 years since 1940**

cues.label: LAKE CHAD BASIN
cues.spoken: Around the shrinking Lake Chad basin, temperatures of thirty degrees Celsius or above have been recorded every single day for the past four weeks, accelerating evaporation at a lake that has already lost vast surface area over recent decades.
cues.ticker: Lake Chad basin **30°C+ every day for 4 weeks** - evaporation accelerating

cues.label: CENTRAL CHAD
cues.spoken: Not a single millimetre of rain has fallen across central Chad in the past fourteen days, against an expected total of nearly thirteen millimetres. The ground is baked dry, and livestock and agriculture face severe stress.
cues.ticker: Central Chad **zero rainfall in 14 days** - Sahel drought **deepening rapidly**

cues.label: SAHEL PRESSURE DOME
cues.spoken: A persistent high-pressure cell at the surface is suppressing any convection and locking the region in heat, preventing the formation of the cloud cover that might otherwise provide some overnight relief.
cues.ticker: Sahel high pressure **blocking all rainfall** - convection **completely suppressed**

cues.label: CENTRAL AFRICAN BORDER
cues.spoken: To the south, the GDACS Orange Drought Alert covers a vast arc from Cameroon and the Central African Republic through to South Sudan, Kenya and Uganda, with the heat dome now extending the impact zone further north into the Sahel.
cues.ticker: GDACS **Orange Drought Alert** - Cameroon to Uganda, **millions affected**

beats.title: Unprecedented Heat Locks Chad and Sahel in Record Warmth
beats.text: An extraordinary heat dome is delivering temperatures of thirty point four degrees Celsius across central Chad tonight - a reading seven point three degrees above the November seasonal normal and the highest anomaly ever recorded here for this date in eighty-seven years of ERA5 data. The heat has been entirely unbroken for a full calendar month, with not a single day of cooler conditions and virtually no rainfall. The Lake Chad basin, already under severe ecological stress from decades of shrinkage, is experiencing accelerated evaporation as a result.

beats.title: Twenty-Eight Days Without Relief - Zero Rain in a Fortnight
beats.text: Every one of the past twenty-eight days has been anomalously hot across the central Chad region, an unbroken streak that ranks as one of the most sustained temperature anomalies ever recorded in the ERA5 archive for this part of the Sahel. No rain whatsoever has fallen in the past fourteen days against an expected total of nearly thirteen millimetres. The combined heat and rainfall deficit is driving acute food and water stress, compounding the GDACS Orange Drought Alert that has been in force across the broader central and eastern African region since May.

beats.title: Number One - Never Been This Hot on This Date
beats.text: The current temperature anomaly ranks number one in the full ERA5 archive at the ninety-ninth point four percentile - truly unprecedented for late November across this region. By comparison, the previous record for extreme late-November heat exceedances across the central African Sahel stood at two events per decade in the nineteen-forties to nineteen-seventies baseline period. That figure has now risen to seven events per decade in the most recent forty years, a more than three-fold increase in extreme heat frequency.

beats.title: Sahel Heat Extremes Multiplying as Rainfall Becomes Less Predictable
beats.text: Local seasonal warming across central Chad has been modest at around zero point zero three degrees Celsius since the nineteen-forties baseline - but the frequency of extreme heat exceedances tells a starkly different story, with the region now seeing seven hot events per decade compared to just two in the earlier period. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change scenarios for the Lake Chad region project worsening climatic instability, including increasingly severe heat episodes and erratic rainfall patterns, with predictions of a further rise of up to four point four degrees Celsius in mean annual temperatures by the end of this century.

stories.kicker: RECORD HEAT · WEST SIBERIA AND KAZAKHSTAN
stories.headline: West Siberia shatters all records as 21°C heat anomaly grips region for an entire month
stories.ticker: **West Siberia heat record smashed** - anomaly **+21.2°C above November normal** - **unprecedented #1 in 87 years since 1940** /// Actual temperature **-2.1°C** where the November normal is **-20.1°C** - a staggering positive departure /// **28 of 28 days** anomalously warm - not a single cold day in **four weeks** /// Novosibirsk reports **warmest November on record** - rain instead of snow across Siberia /// West Siberia regional warming of **1.49°C since the 1940s** - but extreme warm events now **5 per decade** vs just **3 per decade** in the nineteen-forties /// Polar Vortex split in early November linked to this **record warm Siberian ridge**
stories.voice_script: Across western Siberia and northern Kazakhstan, temperatures have soared to nearly twenty-one degrees Celsius above the late-November seasonal normal - the highest anomaly of any kind recorded in this region in eighty-seven years of records since nineteen forty. The actual temperature stands at around minus two degrees Celsius, but for a region where late November should deliver minus twenty, that feels extraordinary. This warmth has held absolutely every single day for the past four weeks. Novosibirsk meteorologists are calling November two thousand and twenty-six the most anomalously warm on record, and Russian media report that instead of customary snow and frost, regions from Kazakhstan northward through Siberia are seeing rain and above-zero conditions.
stories.region: West Siberia, Novosibirsk, Omsk and Northern Kazakhstan

cues.label: WEST SIBERIA CORE
cues.spoken: At the heart of the ridge, temperatures across western Siberia are running more than twenty-one degrees Celsius above the November seasonal normal - the highest anomaly ever recorded here in eighty-seven years, ranking number one in the entire ERA5 archive.
cues.ticker: West Siberia anomaly **+21.2°C** - **#1 in 87 years since 1940** - unprecedented

cues.label: NOVOSIBIRSK
cues.spoken: In Novosibirsk, the mercury is hovering around minus two degrees Celsius - nearly eighteen degrees warmer than the late-November norm. Meteorologists say this is the warmest November on record for the city, with rain falling where snow would usually lie thick on the ground.
cues.ticker: Novosibirsk **warmest November on record** - rain where snow should be

cues.label: NORTHERN KAZAKHSTAN
cues.spoken: Across northern Kazakhstan, rainfall in the past fortnight has reached nearly fourteen millimetres, nearly three times the expected total, as the warm ridge drives moisture into a region that should be in deep winter freeze.
cues.ticker: Northern Kazakhstan **rainfall 3× above expected** - warm ridge driving moisture

cues.label: OMSK AND TYUMEN
cues.spoken: An anomalously strong upper-level ridge is locked across western Siberia, suppressing the normal southward plunge of Arctic air and deflecting the polar vortex into two separate cores - a pattern linked to the earliest recorded stratospheric warming event of the entire satellite era.
cues.ticker: Siberian ridge **deflecting polar vortex** - linked to **earliest SSW on record**

cues.label: EAST KAZAKHSTAN
cues.spoken: Further south into eastern Kazakhstan, the anomaly remains at nearly sixteen degrees above normal, reinforcing the signal that this is a vast, locked warm ridge covering millions of square kilometres of central Eurasia.
cues.ticker: East Kazakhstan **+15.8°C above normal** - warm ridge covers **millions of km²**

beats.title: Western Siberia Records Its Warmest November in History
beats.text: An extraordinary warm ridge is delivering temperatures of minus two degrees Celsius across western Siberia and northern Kazakhstan tonight - regions where the November average is around minus twenty degrees. Russian meteorologists in Novosibirsk describe this as the most anomalously warm November on record, with rainfall instead of snow, and not a single frosty day in the past four weeks. The anomaly of twenty-one point two degrees Celsius above normal represents the highest figure ever recorded here in eighty-seven years of ERA5 data for this calendar date.

beats.title: Twenty-Eight Consecutive Days of Unprecedented Warmth
beats.text: Every single one of the past twenty-eight days has been anomalously warm across western Siberia and northern Kazakhstan, an unbroken streak of exceptional warmth that is entirely without precedent in the modern observational record for this region and season. The fourteen-day rainfall total stands at thirteen point eight millimetres against an expected five millimetres, confirming that the warm ridge is also carrying moisture that would normally have been locked out by frozen air masses. Russian synoptic meteorologists attribute the heat to warm air masses flowing northward from Central Asia, locked in place by an unusually persistent atmospheric circulation pattern.

beats.title: Number One in 87 Years - Genuinely Unprecedented
beats.text: The temperature anomaly of twenty-one point two degrees Celsius ranks number one at the ninety-ninth point four percentile in the full ERA5 archive - a figure that is genuinely unprecedented for late November across western Siberia. The seasonal normal for the region is minus twenty point one degrees Celsius; the actual observed temperature of minus two degrees represents the largest positive departure from normal ever recorded here at any point in the eighty-seven-year archive. This event has also been linked by forecasters to the earliest sudden stratospheric warming on record in the polar vortex, which split into two separate cores in early November.

beats.title: Siberian Warming Accelerating Arctic Amplification
beats.text: Local seasonal warming of one point four nine degrees Celsius since the nineteen-forties baseline reflects the broader process of Arctic amplification, by which the high-latitude regions are warming two to three times faster than the global average. The frequency of extreme warm events across western Siberia has risen from three per decade in the nineteen-forties to nineteen-seventies period to five per decade in the most recent forty years. Scientists have long identified western Siberia as one of the fastest-warming regions on Earth, with consequences including thawing permafrost, methane release, and the disruption of the jet stream patterns that govern weather across the entire Northern Hemisphere.
